Comparing TaskNet and O*NET Task Inventories

Source: vignettes/tasknet-comparison.Rmd
tasknet-comparison.Rmd

Stanford’s TaskNet elicits workers’ accounts of their jobs and combines them into occupational task statements. Its public pilot compares 202 TaskNet statements with 118 O*NET statements across six occupations. The Stanford publication abstract identifies that comparison release as 31.0; the CSV itself has no release version field. It is an alternative inventory, not an official O*NET release or a representative inventory of the entire workforce.

onet_tasknet_read() reads a CSV you already have. It does not download, cache, match statements by similarity, or estimate exposure. onet_tasknet_relations() expands the supplied comparison links without inventing allocation weights.

Start with a synthetic file

Every statement and rating in this example is stylized. The bundled CSV is invented to demonstrate the format. Neither its task statements nor its numerical results are findings about real occupations.

path <- system.file("extdata", "tasknet-synthetic.csv", package = "onet2r")
tasks <- onet_tasknet_read(path, as_of = "synthetic teaching fixture")

counts <- tasks |> count(inventory, name = "statements")
stopifnot(
  nrow(tasks) == 9L,
  sum(tasks$inventory == "TaskNet") == 5L,
  sum(tasks$inventory == "O*NET") == 4L,
  n_distinct(tasks$onet_soc_code) == 2L
)
knitr::kable(counts)
inventory statements
O*NET 4
TaskNet 5

The expected inventory counts are 5 and 4, with nine unique study IDs. study_task_id identifies a record within the study file. Even an O*NET-labelled comparison row has a study ID, not an official archive task_id. The onet_soc_code column retains eight-digit occupational detail. Do not join study IDs directly to official archive Task IDs.

Expand explicit relationships 

links <- onet_tasknet_relations(tasks)
stopifnot(
  nrow(links) == 5L,
  sum(links$relation_type == "refines") == 3L,
  sum(links$relation_type == "overlaps") == 2L
)
links |>
  select(from_study_task_id, to_study_task_id, relation_type) |>
  knitr::kable()
from_study_task_id to_study_task_id relation_type
S-FIX-01 O-FIX-01 refines
S-FIX-02 O-FIX-01 refines
S-FIX-02 O-FIX-02 refines
S-FIX-03 O-FIX-02 overlaps
S-AUX-01 O-AUX-01 overlaps

All edges point from TaskNet to the comparison inventory. A refined_by declaration on a comparison row is the inverse of refines on a TaskNet row. Reciprocal declarations describe one edge, not two. An overlap is stored in the same canonical direction for convenience, not because it is causal. Different relation types on one pair remain separate edges. Count distinct endpoint pairs explicitly if that, rather than typed edges, is the denominator.

There are three refinement edges but only two refining TaskNet statements in this example. One statement can refine several others, and several statements can refine the same one. Expanding links and then averaging joined ratings would give some statements extra weight.

refining <- links |>
  filter(relation_type == "refines") |>
  distinct(from_study_task_id)
stopifnot(nrow(refining) == 2L)

Create links from the complete, unchanged reader result before selecting an inventory or occupation subset. The relation helper rejects edited or subset input, even when a subset would contain every endpoint it needs. Missing targets, nonreciprocal declarations, and region labels that disagree with links are errors, not cases the reader silently repairs.

Describe differences without inventing time change 

summary <- tasks |>
  summarise(
    statements = n(),
    mean_importance = mean(importance),
    .by = inventory
  )
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    summary$mean_importance[summary$inventory == "TaskNet"], 3.6
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    summary$mean_importance[summary$inventory == "O*NET"], 3.25
  ))
)
knitr::kable(summary, digits = 2)
inventory statements mean_importance
TaskNet 5 3.60
O*NET 4 3.25 

unmatched <- tasks |>
  filter(region %in% c("new", "missing")) |>
  select(inventory, region, study_task_id, task)
stopifnot(nrow(unmatched) == 2L)
knitr::kable(unmatched)
inventory region study_task_id task
TaskNet new S-FIX-04 Stylized: document a fixture exception.
O*NET missing O-FIX-03 Stylized: archive a fixture record.

The expected means are 3.60 and 3.25 for two different stylized statement sets. This is not a matched comparison, a significance test, or a change over time. Inventory construction, statement granularity, and rating samples can all affect such summaries. On real data, disclose missing-rating counts and denominators rather than silently dropping observations. Duration, training, articulability, verifiability, and top-worker gap are TaskNet-only fields in the inspected public snapshot; all 118 comparison records have missing values for each. Those fields cannot support a two-inventory rating comparison.

The source’s new and missing labels describe matches between inventories. They do not date the emergence or disappearance of work. TaskNet relevance is not a time share, and published frequency and duration ratings do not automatically supply time-allocation weights.

Read a manually acquired public file

Obtain the CSV through the Stanford project page. Keep the original file and record its actual acquisition time. The following code is not executed during builds:

tasks <- onet_tasknet_read(
  "tasknet-data.csv",
  source_url = paste0(
    "https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/",
    "app/uploads/2026/10/tasknet-data.csv"
  ),
  as_of = "your recorded source snapshot"
)
links <- onet_tasknet_relations(tasks)

The reader records the SHA-256 of the bytes it parses. A source URL or snapshot label supplied by the caller is a provenance assertion, not independently verified publication metadata. Reading a local file does not establish when it was downloaded. A digest identifies bytes, not a license or a guarantee of scientific validity.

Do not bundle or redistribute the real CSV until its terms are confirmed. The TaskNet system repository has its own licensing statements and synthetic validation inputs. Those do not establish redistribution rights for Stanford’s separate public CSV.

Keep downstream measures explicit

onet_measure() can validate user-supplied scores keyed to study_task_id. Do not manufacture Core/Supplemental labels to pass TaskNet data through onet_task_to_occupation(), whose contract expects O*NET task metadata. No new aggregation method or exposure score is introduced here.

The CSV’s research-score columns are retained as source fields, not endorsed or selected as defaults. Official archive readers and longitudinal reconciliation remain separate from this cross-inventory comparison.

Source: Wang, Haupt, Robinson, Lewis, Brynjolfsson, and Yang (2026), TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale. Definitions above are limited to the accessible Stanford project documentation and public CSV.
